context:
Patient: 59F, breast cancer survivor (2016: dose-dense AC, cumulative doxorubicin 240 mg/m2, left breast RT, on anastrozole), presents with left axillary mass, fevers to 38.4 C, drenching night sweats; ECOG 1, LDH 510. Non-GCB DLBCL (MYC 45%, BCL2 70%, FISH negative for rearrangements), PET nodes above and below the diaphragm plus splenic nodules, marrow negative, and new LVEF 45% (62% in 2016) with GLS -14%.
What this case tests: Spleen is a nodal site under Lugano, so stage is III, not IV, and IPI is 2. | Double-expressor by IHC but FISH-negative, so not double-hit; no intensification to DA-EPOCH-R. | Prior doxorubicin 240 mg/m2, left chest RT and LVEF 62% to 45% mean standard full-dose R-CHOP / Pola-R-CHP is not safe as is. | Treatment must stay curative: anthracycline-free (R-CEOP / R-GCVP) or cardio-protected regimen, with cardio-oncology input and cardioprotective drugs. | CNS-IPI 2 with no high-risk sites: no routine CNS prophylaxis.

answer.diagnosis: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), not otherwise specified (NOS), non-germinal-center B-cell phenotype by the Hans algorithm (CD10 negative, BCL6 positive, MUM1 positive), with a double-expressor immunophenotype (MYC about 45%, BCL2 about 70%) but no MYC, BCL2 or BCL6 rearrangement by FISH (not double-hit/triple-hit); EBV-negative, Ki-67 about 80%. No bone marrow involvement. History of left breast invasive ductal carcinoma (2016, pT2 pN0, ER-positive/HER2-negative), in remission; the axillary biopsy shows lymphoma with negative cytokeratin and GATA3, excluding breast cancer recurrence.
answer.stage: Lugano/Ann Arbor stage IIIB: lymph node involvement above and below the diaphragm (left axillary, mediastinal, mesenteric, para-aortic) with splenic involvement; B symptoms (documented fever to 38.4 C and drenching night sweats; weight loss about 3%, below the 10% B-symptom threshold). No non-lymphatic extranodal organ involvement. Largest mass is a 7.5 cm mesenteric conglomerate, not bulky by the conventional >=10 cm criterion. IPI 2 (stage III and elevated LDH) = low-intermediate risk; age-adjusted IPI 2 = high-intermediate; CNS-IPI 2 = intermediate.
answer.biology: DLBCL NOS with non-GCB/Hans phenotype and double-expressor biology (MYC and BCL2 by IHC), high proliferation (Ki-67 80%), high LDH (510 U/L), beta-2 microglobulin 2.9 mg/L, and B symptoms. FISH is negative for MYC, BCL2 and BCL6 rearrangements, so this is not a double-hit or triple-hit lymphoma; EBER is negative. The phenotype predicts a somewhat inferior PFS/OS than generic DLBCL but does not change standard first-line therapy outside a clinical trial. There is no morphologic or immunophenotypic evidence of transformed follicular lymphoma or metastatic breast carcinoma.
answer.prognosis: Potentially curable with anthracycline-based immunochemotherapy. With IPI 2 (low-intermediate; age-adjusted IPI 2 high-intermediate), expected 5-year PFS/OS is roughly 60-75% with R-CHOP-type therapy, with the double-expressor phenotype and high Ki-67 as adverse modifiers. CNS relapse risk is about 4-5% at 2 years by CNS-IPI 2, but there are no high-risk CNS sites. The main competing risk is anthracycline cardiomyopathy (baseline LVEF 45% after prior doxorubicin 240 mg/m2 and left breast radiotherapy); cardiac events could compromise both cure and survival.
answer.first_line_treatment: Curative-intent R-CHOP x6 every 21 days: rituximab 375 mg/m2 IV day 1, cyclophosphamide 750 mg/m2 IV day 1, doxorubicin 50 mg/m2 IV day 1 with dexrazoxane 500 mg/m2 IV immediately before each doxorubicin dose (10:1), vincristine 1.4 mg/m2 IV day 1 (cap 2 mg), prednisone 100 mg PO daily days 1-5. I choose R-CHOP plus dexrazoxane rather than Pola-R-CHP. Pola-R-CHP is NCCN category 1 for IPI 2-5, but she has LVEF 45% after prior doxorubicin (cumulative 240 mg/m2) and left breast radiotherapy; six R-CHOP cycles will add 300 mg/m2, bringing cumulative doxorubicin to about 540 mg/m2. POLARIX enrolled patients with adequate cardiac function, and patients with LVEF 45% were not represented; Pola-R-CHP also does not reduce anthracycline exposure. I would reconsider Pola-R-CHP only if cardiology considers her optimized and she places high value on its modest PFS advantage. If dexrazoxane is unavailable, or if LVEF falls modestly but remains >40%, non-pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (R-COMP) is my preferred anthracycline substitution; if symptomatic heart failure or LVEF <40% develops, I will switch to a non-anthracycline regimen (e.g., R-CEOP) rather than simply dose-reduce. I will not plan consolidative radiotherapy upfront for the 7.5 cm mesenteric mass (below the conventional >=10 cm bulky threshold); I will decide after the end-of-treatment PET, reserving RT for a residual PET-positive site. No CNS prophylaxis. Stop anastrozole now, since she is at the planned end of a 10-year course (November 2026) and continuation through cytotoxic therapy adds no benefit.
answer.cns_risk: CNS-IPI 2 (stage III and elevated LDH; age 59, ECOG 1, no more than one extranodal site, no kidney/adrenal involvement) = intermediate risk, approximately 4-5% at 2 years. She has no high-risk CNS sites (no testicular, breast, adrenal, kidney, bone marrow, epidural or sinonasal involvement) and no double-hit/triple-hit rearrangement. I will not give intrathecal chemotherapy or high-dose methotrexate prophylaxis and will not perform a routine lumbar puncture. I would change this if bone marrow, testis, breast, adrenal, kidney or epidural involvement were found, or if FISH showed a double-hit lymphoma, in which case I would add CNS-directed prophylaxis and consider an intensive regimen.
answer.response_assessment: Interim FDG PET/CT after 2 cycles (for prognosis and to confirm response before committing to 6 cycles; I will not escalate or de-escalate solely on an interim Deauville 4 without biopsy) and end-of-treatment FDG PET/CT 6-8 weeks after cycle 6, interpreted by Lugano 2014/Deauville 5-point criteria. Deauville 1-3 = complete metabolic response; Deauville 4-5 = residual disease, with biopsy of the dominant site (especially the mesenteric mass) to distinguish viable lymphoma from inflammation. If complete response, surveillance without routine imaging. If biopsy-proven residual disease, second-line platinum-based salvage (R-ICE, R-DHAP or R-GDP) followed by autologous transplant if chemo-sensitive; CAR-T or a clinical trial if refractory. Repeat echocardiogram at the end of therapy and as directed by cardio-oncology.
answer.pretreatment_workup: Already completed: staging FDG PET/CT, bone marrow aspirate/biopsy, FISH, IHC, echocardiogram, CBC/CMP/LDH/urate/beta-2 microglobulin, HIV/HBV/HCV serologies, and ECOG status. Before cycle 1 I still want: cardiology consultation with ECG, troponin and BNP/NT-proBNP, and consideration of cardiac MRI to define the cardiomyopathy; optimization of blood pressure and guideline-directed heart-failure therapy; a repeat CBC/CMP/LDH/urate immediately before treatment; dental evaluation; G6PD testing if rasburicase may be used; and a plan for HBV vaccination (she is anti-HBs negative). I do not need a routine lumbar puncture, fertility preservation, or repeat bone marrow. I would send the pathology for expert review only if there were diagnostic uncertainty; it is not required for this unequivocal DLBCL.
answer.supportive_care: Tumor lysis prophylaxis with allopurinol 300 mg daily (renal function is normal) plus IV hydration, with monitoring of potassium, calcium, phosphate, uric acid and creatinine before and 24-48 hours after the first cycles; rasburicase if uric acid rises markedly or the risk is judged high (check G6PD first). Primary febrile neutropenia prophylaxis with pegfilgrastim 6 mg SC day 2. Antiemetics with a 5-HT3 antagonist plus dexamethasone (add olanzapine or an NK1 antagonist if needed). PJP prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole three times weekly during therapy (her penicillin allergy is not a contraindication). Continue amlodipine, add an ACE inhibitor/ARB and a beta-blocker for LVEF 45%/hypertension per cardiology, and avoid fluid overload. Dexrazoxane with each doxorubicin dose. Stop anastrozole; continue calcium/vitamin D and monitor bone health. Inactivated influenza, pneumococcal and COVID vaccination; avoid live vaccines during rituximab; give HBV vaccine when immunologically appropriate. Counsel about fever, neutropenia, TLS symptoms, and avoid acetaminophen masking fever. Social work/psychosocial support for return to work; the husband is a reliable caregiver.
answer.fitness_and_goals: ECOG 1, age 59, working full-time and independent, with normal renal, hepatic and marrow function; she is fit for curative full-dose immunochemotherapy. The only major vulnerability is the anthracycline-exposed heart (LVEF 45%, reduced GLS, hypertension, family history of heart failure), which makes cardiac protection and cardio-oncology co-management central. Her stated goal is cure and return to work, so I will treat with curative intent rather than palliate or watch-and-wait. If she develops symptomatic heart failure or LVEF <40%, or if her performance status declines substantially, I will reassess and switch to a non-anthracycline regimen; if she were frail or preferred quality of life over intensive therapy, R-miniCHOP or palliative immunochemotherapy would be appropriate.
missing_information: Cardiology consultation with baseline ECG, troponin and BNP/NT-proBNP, plus consideration of cardiac MRI to define whether LVEF 45% is anthracycline/radiation-related and to guide heart-failure therapy.
Prior left breast radiotherapy treatment plan/dosimetry to estimate cardiac radiation dose and assess coronary/valvular risk.
G6PD status, needed before rasburicase if tumor lysis prophylaxis escalates.
Documented infectious workup for the fevers (e.g., blood cultures) before starting corticosteroids, although the fevers are most consistent with lymphoma B symptoms.
HBV vaccination plan/documentation of immunity (anti-HBs is negative).
Availability and eligibility for clinical trials or molecular profiling (e.g., TP53, MYD88, CD79B), which could inform prognosis but is not required for standard therapy.
Baseline dental evaluation and any need for pre-chemotherapy dental work.
Patient preferences regarding intensity of therapy, travel/work schedule and cardiology follow-up, to finalize shared decision-making.

items.criterion: The response states the diagnosis is diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (NOS) with a non-germinal-center (non-GCB) phenotype by the Hans algorithm.
The response notes that Hans non-GCB is an immunohistochemical surrogate and is not equivalent to molecular ABC cell-of-origin by gene-expression profiling.
The response states the left axillary node is lymphoma and not recurrent breast carcinoma (cytokeratin AE1/AE3 and GATA3 negative).
The response stages the disease as Lugano/Ann Arbor stage III (nodes on both sides of the diaphragm with splenic involvement).
The response explains that the spleen is lymphatic tissue (a nodal site), so splenic nodules do not make the disease stage IV, and that there is no non-lymphatic extranodal or marrow involvement.
The response notes B symptoms (documented fevers >38 C and drenching night sweats).
The response notes the 7.5 cm mass is below the 10 cm Lugano bulk threshold, acknowledging that bulk definitions vary (some trials use 7.5 cm).
The response stages this patient as stage IV (e.g. by counting splenic involvement as extranodal disease).
The response classifies the lymphoma as double-expressor by IHC (MYC 45% >=40%, BCL2 70% >=50%) but NOT double-hit (FISH shows no MYC, BCL2 or BCL6 rearrangement).
The response classifies this lymphoma as double-hit / high-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 rearrangements.
The response recommends DA-EPOCH-R (or another intensified regimen) on the basis of double-expressor biology.
The response calculates IPI as 2 (low-intermediate risk): elevated LDH and stage III; age 59, ECOG 1 and no extranodal sites (spleen is not counted as extranodal) score zero.
The response calculates CNS-IPI as 2 (intermediate risk).
The response states that routine CNS prophylaxis is not indicated (CNS-IPI 2, no kidney/adrenal, testicular or breast involvement).
The response mandates CNS prophylaxis (high-dose methotrexate or intrathecal therapy) for this patient.

The response recognizes anthracycline-related cardiac risk (prior doxorubicin 240 mg/m2, left chest radiotherapy, LVEF fall from 62% to 45%, i.e. cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction) and does NOT plan standard full-dose doxorubicin (R-CHOP or Pola-R-CHP) without first addressing cardiac function.

The response recommends standard R-CHOP or Pola-R-CHP (full-dose doxorubicin) without conditioning it on the reduced LVEF / prior anthracycline exposure (e.g. without cardio-oncology clearance, a cardioprotective modification, or a non-anthracycline alternative).
The response requests urgent cardio-oncology (or cardiology) evaluation before starting therapy.
The response starts or optimizes guideline-directed cardioprotective therapy: an ACE inhibitor/ARB (or ARNI) plus a beta-blocker (e.g. carvedilol), for example replacing amlodipine.

The response recommends a curative-intent anthracycline-free or anthracycline-modified regimen, e.g. R-CEOP (etoposide in place of doxorubicin) or R-GCVP; R-CHOP with liposomal doxorubicin or dexrazoxane is acceptable only if conditioned on cardio-oncology judging it safe.
The response acknowledges that anthracycline-free regimens likely have lower efficacy than anthracycline-based therapy.
The response plans serial cardiac monitoring during therapy: repeat LVEF/GLS imaging plus troponin and/or natriuretic peptide (BNP/NT-proBNP).
The response recommends palliative-only treatment, best supportive care, or hospice as the plan.
The response plans an end-of-treatment FDG PET-CT read with Lugano criteria / Deauville 5-point scale.
The response assesses tumor lysis risk as low-intermediate (normal creatinine and uric acid, LDH ~2x ULN) and gives allopurinol with hydration for cycle 1.
The response recommends (or reasonably considers) primary G-CSF support with each cycle.
The response addresses the ongoing anastrozole: continuing it is acceptable (no meaningful interaction), or holding it in coordination with breast oncology is also acceptable.
The response confirms hepatitis B serology was checked (HBsAg and anti-HBc nonreactive) before rituximab.
The response judges the patient fit for curative-intent therapy (ECOG 1, normal organ function apart from the LVEF) and acknowledges her goal of cure.
The response lists the cause of the LVEF decline / cardio-oncology work-up as missing (e.g. ischemic evaluation given prior left chest radiotherapy, cardiac MRI, baseline troponin and NT-proBNP).
